newsitem.title: USA: Sept muni futures expiration no replay of June.
newsitem.headline: Sept muni futures expiration no replay of June.

text.p: The sharp run-up on index bonds that preceeded the expiration of the June municipal futures contract was absent Wednesday as the market neared Thursday's September contract expiration, traders said.
Meanwhile, the Chicago Board of Trade declined to comment on reports that it had stepped up surveillance ahead of the September contract's expiration.
"We still think some of the index bonds are overpriced but it's certainly not as blatant as it was last time," one market source said.
A trader at another firm described pricing as fair.
"We think the current pricing is reasonably fair," he said. "There's some sectors of the index that we think are a little cheap, some that are rich, but nothing outstanding or outrageous."
Another trader, however, said he was looking for index bonds to underperform the broader market.

"I think that the last run up was done by one person, maybe two, but primarily one person who chose not to get involved in that trade this time around. And secondly, there were a lot of people that went long index bonds because they always outperform at expiration."
Those who banked on a run-up in index bonds may have a hard time finding buyers for them, the trader said, adding that he observed a substantial amount of index bonds out for the bid Wednesday.

"People always assume that what happened time A will happen time B, and that assumption has caused them to take defensive measures to protect against what happened last time," the trader said. "Only it didn't happen, so now they are going to lose money another way."

Back in June, a sharp run up in bonds contained in the Bond Buyer 40-bond index ignited controversy in the municipal market. Traders pointed to a single buyer--Susquehanna Capital Corp, and speculated that the firm was long the June contract and trying to enhance its value by bidding up index bonds. The contract is cash-settled at the price of the index on expiration.
Susquehanna, however, said it was just engaged in normal hedging activity.

"Nothing out of the ordinary happened that doesn't occur in many stock and bond futures expirations," Joel Greenberg, a managing director with the Philadelphia-based firm, said at the time. "You can always find an unhappy trader after any expiration."

Some market players found no problem with Susquehanna's strategy, saying the firm honored its bids. One trader outside the firm said those who thought Susquehanna's bids were too high should have hit them.

Others, however, said while Susquehanna did nothing illegal, its actions could cause some to question the contract's validity because they may create the appearance that the contract can be manipulated.
In the wake of the controversy, the CBOT together with its Muncipal Bond Advisory Committee have been taking a hard look at ways to improve the contract.
A CBOT spokesman Wednesday, however, declined to comment on reports that the CBOT was questioning traders about their September positions.

"If it's concerning any kind of market surveillance, that's not something we can talk about," CBOT spokeswoman Kiki Melonides said. "All I can say is that we monitor all our contracts," she said, adding that CBOT heightens monitoring during expiration.
One trader said CBOT questioned him and others about September positions.
"They wanted to know if anybody's going to run up the index, so they called everybody who had a position long or short and asked them what are their intentions."
Other traders said they had been in touch with the CBOT officials in recent days but received no unusual queries of late.
--Kathie O'Donnell, 212-859-1650
